claims.text: Optimizing tempering temperature and duration in a conventional martensitic steel can reproducibly induce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition over a narrow temperature window.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition is reversible.
Carbide precipitation during tempering can temporarily reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Impurity segregation, potentially involving phosphorus, can temporarily reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Temporary reduction of grain-boundary cohesion produces a pronounced loss of ductility.
The as-quenched martensitic steel has a supersaturated and relatively homogeneous microstructure before tailored tempering.
Systematically varying tempering temperature and duration will produce distinct microstructural states.
Tempering forms and redistributes fine carbide precipitates.
Tempering causes minor embrittling impurities such as phosphorus to segregate at grain boundaries.
Intermediate tempering conditions generate a microstructure with reduced grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion at intermediate tempering conditions causes a transient embrittled state.
At lower testing temperatures, the microstructure is insufficiently evolved and ductile deformation dominates.
At higher testing temperatures, the microstructure is over-tempered and ductile deformation dominates.
Tempered martensitic steel will show a statistically significant and reproducible dip in ductility within a narrow temperature range.
The narrow temperature range will also show a corresponding dip in fracture toughness.
Ductility will be higher immediately below and above the embrittlement window.
Conventionally tempered martensitic steels used as the baseline do not exhibit a sharp, narrow drop in ductility.
The proposed transition occurs only in conventional tempered martensitic steels.
Comparable behavior is not anticipated in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys engineered to avoid temper embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The intervention attributes microstructural evolution to tempering temperature and duration, but the mechanism attributes insufficient evolution or over-tempering to lower or higher mechanical testing temperatures. The hypothesis does not clarify whether the narrow window refers to tempering temperature, testing temperature, or both.
